rubric: A receipt proves payment; the seller issues it to the buyer confirming that money has been received.

subject: Commerce
stem: A goods received note (GRN) is prepared by the
options: seller when goods leave|buyer when goods arrive, to confirm the quantity and condition of goods received|bank|insurance company
answer: buyer when goods arrive, to confirm the quantity and condition of goods received
rubric: The GRN (delivery note signed by the buyer) confirms receipt of goods and is used to check against the invoice.

subject: Commerce
stem: The order in which business documents are typically used in a trade transaction is
options: Invoice → order → quotation → delivery|Enquiry → quotation → order → invoice → delivery → statement|Delivery → invoice → order → quotation|Payment → invoice → delivery → order
answer: Enquiry → quotation → order → invoice → delivery → statement
rubric: Trade sequence: buyer makes enquiry → seller sends quotation → buyer sends order → seller sends invoice → goods delivered → statement.

subject: Commerce
stem: A bill of exchange is drawn by the
options: debtor on the creditor|creditor on the debtor, ordering payment of a sum at a future date|bank on the importer|insurer on the trader
answer: creditor on the debtor, ordering payment of a sum at a future date
rubric: A bill of exchange: the drawer (creditor) directs the drawee (debtor) to pay a sum to the payee at a future date.

subject: Commerce
stem: A consignment note accompanies goods transported by road or rail and serves as
options: proof of insurance|evidence of the contract of carriage between the consignor and carrier|a tax receipt|an export licence
answer: evidence of the contract of carriage between the consignor and carrier
rubric: The consignment note (road/rail waybill) identifies the goods, parties and delivery terms in the transport contract.

subject: Commerce
stem: The purpose of a catalogue in trade is to
options: show the seller's bank balance|provide a comprehensive list of available goods with descriptions and prices to attract buyers|prove ownership of goods|settle disputes
answer: provide a comprehensive list of available goods with descriptions and prices to attract buyers
rubric: Catalogues are marketing tools that describe all goods/services, their specifications and prices for prospective buyers.

subject: Commerce
stem: Which document is used to authorise customs clearance for imported goods?
options: Bill of lading|Invoice|Bill of entry (import declaration)|Certificate of origin
answer: Bill of entry (import declaration)
rubric: The bill of entry is submitted to customs with supporting documents; customs processes it and authorises release of goods.

subject: Commerce
stem: A delivery note accompanies goods being delivered and is signed by the buyer to confirm
options: payment has been made|that goods have been received in good condition|that insurance is in place|the shipping route
answer: that goods have been received in good condition
rubric: A signed delivery note proves the buyer received the goods; disputes about non-delivery or damage rely on this document.

subject: Commerce
stem: A pro-forma invoice is used when
options: payment is already made|goods are sent on approval or in advance of regular trading, providing the buyer with price information|goods are damaged|a return is being made
answer: goods are sent on approval or in advance of regular trading, providing the buyer with price information
rubric: A proforma invoice is a preliminary bill of sale; it is not a demand for payment but provides price/shipping details.

subject: Commerce
stem: Which document allows an importer to defer payment for goods to a future agreed date?
options: Receipt|Credit note|Bill of exchange (accepted)|Purchase order
answer: Bill of exchange (accepted)
rubric: When a buyer (drawee) accepts a bill of exchange, they commit to paying the stated sum at the future maturity date.

subject: Commerce
stem: The terms "FOB" (Free On Board) in a trade contract mean that
options: the seller pays all costs to the buyer's destination|the seller pays costs and risk up to loading onto the ship; buyer pays from there|the buyer pays everything|insurance is included
answer: the seller pays costs and risk up to loading onto the ship; buyer pays from there
rubric: FOB: seller is responsible for goods up to the named port of shipment and loading onto the vessel; risk transfers to buyer on loading.

subject: Commerce
stem: CIF (Cost, Insurance and Freight) means
options: buyer pays all costs|the seller pays the cost of goods, marine insurance and freight to the named destination port|only cost is included|only freight is included
answer: the seller pays the cost of goods, marine insurance and freight to the named destination port
rubric: Under CIF, the seller quotes a price inclusive of the cost of goods, marine insurance premium and freight charges.

subject: Commerce
stem: An airway bill differs from a bill of lading in that
options: they are identical|an airway bill is non-negotiable and cannot transfer title of goods|a bill of lading is for road transport|an airway bill is for sea transport
answer: an airway bill is non-negotiable and cannot transfer title of goods
rubric: Unlike a bill of lading (which can transfer ownership), an airway bill is a receipt/contract only — it is non-negotiable.

subject: Commerce
stem: The purpose of a statement of account sent by a creditor at month-end is to
options: place a new order|summarise all invoices, payments and credits to arrive at the net balance owed|confirm insurance|update the delivery schedule
answer: summarise all invoices, payments and credits to arrive at the net balance owed
rubric: Monthly statements show all transactions, credits, debits and the closing balance; they remind debtors of amounts outstanding.

subject: Commerce
stem: Which of the following is NOT a source document for bookkeeping?
options: Invoice|Receipt|Credit note|Company chairman's speech
answer: Company chairman's speech
rubric: Source documents (invoices, receipts, credit notes, bank statements) initiate accounting entries; a speech is not a financial record.

subject: Commerce
stem: A debit note is sometimes used by a buyer to inform the seller that
options: payment has been received|the seller has been debited in the buyer's books (e.g. for returned goods)|new goods are required|a discount was received
answer: the seller has been debited in the buyer's books (e.g. for returned goods)
rubric: When a buyer returns goods, they issue a debit note to the seller, reducing the amount payable.

subject: Commerce
stem: The seller's catalogue shows the full (list) price. The price the buyer actually pays after trade discount is shown on the
options: catalogue|invoice|delivery note|warehouse receipt
answer: invoice
rubric: The invoice shows the net price after applying any trade discount to the catalogue list price.

subject: Commerce
stem: A warranty in a sales contract is
options: a promise by the buyer to pay|a guarantee by the seller about the quality or condition of the goods sold|a type of tariff|a form of insurance
answer: a guarantee by the seller about the quality or condition of the goods sold
rubric: A warranty is a seller's assurance that the product meets certain standards; breach entitles the buyer to remedy.

subject: Commerce
stem: An indent is a document used in foreign trade where an agent in one country places an order on behalf of a buyer in another country. It is essentially a
options: bill of lading|purchase order placed through an agent|delivery note|customs declaration
answer: purchase order placed through an agent
rubric: An indent authorises an overseas agent or buying house to purchase specified goods on behalf of the importer.

subject: Commerce
stem: The Consumer Protection Council (CPC) in Nigeria is responsible for
options: issuing company licences|protecting consumers against hazardous goods, unfair trade practices and deceptive advertising|banking regulation|tax collection
answer: protecting consumers against hazardous goods, unfair trade practices and deceptive advertising
rubric: The CPC (now Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission - FCCPC) enforces consumer rights in Nigeria.

subject: Commerce
stem: Consumer rights include all of the following EXCEPT
options: the right to safety|the right to information|the right to exploit producers|the right to redress
answer: the right to exploit producers
rubric: Consumer rights (UN Guidelines): safety, information, choice, redress, representation, education, healthy environment. Not to exploit others.

subject: Commerce
stem: Caveat emptor means
options: let the seller beware|let the buyer beware (buyer should check goods before purchase)|goods are free of defects|government guarantees quality
answer: let the buyer beware (buyer should check goods before purchase)
rubric: Caveat emptor (Latin): the buyer is responsible for checking the quality of goods before purchase; contrasted with caveat venditor.

subject: Commerce
stem: The Standards Organisation of Nigeria (SON) is responsible for
options: selling imported goods|setting and enforcing quality standards for products sold in Nigeria|managing insurance|running the stock exchange
answer: setting and enforcing quality standards for products sold in Nigeria
rubric: SON sets Nigerian Industrial Standards (NIS), tests products and certifies compliance, protecting consumers from substandard goods.

subject: Commerce
stem: The National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC) regulates
options: banking products|financial investments|food, drugs, cosmetics, medical devices, chemicals and other regulated products|transport companies
answer: food, drugs, cosmetics, medical devices, chemicals and other regulated products
rubric: NAFDAC registers, controls and ensures safety and quality of food, drugs and other regulated consumer products in Nigeria.

subject: Commerce
stem: Business ethics refers to
options: tax avoidance strategies|the moral principles and standards of conduct that guide behaviour in business|how to maximise profit at all costs|government regulations
answer: the moral principles and standards of conduct that guide behaviour in business
rubric: Business ethics: applying ethical principles (honesty, fairness, responsibility) to business decisions and relationships.

subject: Commerce
stem: Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) means
options: a company avoids paying taxes|a company voluntarily contributes to social welfare beyond its legal obligations (e.g. community development, environment)|a company maximises profit only|government aid to companies
answer: a company voluntarily contributes to social welfare beyond its legal obligations (e.g. community development, environment)
rubric: CSR: businesses voluntarily take responsibility for their social and environmental impact, not just shareholder returns.

subject: Commerce
stem: Counterfeit goods harm consumers primarily because
options: they are cheaper|they are made to look like genuine products but are of inferior quality, often unsafe|they are always imported|they are always more expensive
answer: they are made to look like genuine products but are of inferior quality, often unsafe
rubric: Counterfeiting deceives consumers; fake medicines, electronics and foods can be dangerous and have no quality guarantee.

subject: Commerce
stem: A consumer cooperative is formed to
options: maximise individual profit|allow members to pool resources to buy goods in bulk at lower prices for their mutual benefit|manufacture goods for export|regulate trade
answer: allow members to pool resources to buy goods in bulk at lower prices for their mutual benefit
rubric: Consumer cooperatives bulk-buy goods and pass savings on to members, reducing individual cost of living.

subject: Commerce
stem: Misleading advertising is unethical because
options: it increases production costs|it makes false claims that deceive consumers into purchasing unsuitable or harmful products|it reduces profits|it always reduces prices
answer: it makes false claims that deceive consumers into purchasing unsuitable or harmful products
rubric: Deceptive ads violate consumer rights to accurate information and can lead to financial harm or physical danger.

subject: Commerce
stem: The term "planned obsolescence" refers to
options: making products that last forever|designing products to become outdated or non-functional within a planned time to encourage repeat purchases|reducing waste|lowering production costs
answer: designing products to become outdated or non-functional within a planned time to encourage repeat purchases
rubric: Planned obsolescence ensures consumers must replace products sooner; it has been criticised as wasteful and anti-consumer.

subject: Commerce
stem: Price fixing (a form of cartel behaviour) is illegal because
options: it benefits consumers|it involves competitors agreeing to set prices artificially high, reducing competition and harming consumers|it reduces prices|it stabilises employment
answer: it involves competitors agreeing to set prices artificially high, reducing competition and harming consumers
rubric: Price fixing violates competition law; cartels eliminate competition, keeping prices artificially high at consumers' expense.

subject: Commerce
stem: A consumer association advises its members to
options: buy as much as possible|compare prices, read labels and demand quality standards, enabling informed purchasing decisions|avoid saving|only buy luxury goods
answer: compare prices, read labels and demand quality standards, enabling informed purchasing decisions
rubric: Consumer associations empower buyers with information, comparative tests and advocacy, strengthening their market position.

subject: Commerce
stem: Sustainable consumption means
options: consuming as many resources as possible|meeting current needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs|buying only imported goods|using goods until they break
answer: meeting current needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs
rubric: Sustainable consumption applies the sustainability principle to personal and business purchasing — minimising resource depletion.

subject: Commerce
stem: Which of the following best illustrates a conflict of interest in business?
options: A manager recommending a supplier owned by their own relative|An employee arriving at work on time|A company paying taxes|A business expanding its product range
answer: A manager recommending a supplier owned by their own relative
rubric: A conflict of interest arises when a person's private interest could improperly influence their official duties.

subject: Accounting
stem: Accounting is best defined as the
options: process of recording only cash transactions|systematic process of recording, classifying, summarising and communicating financial information for decision-making|filing of tax returns|preparation of budgets only
answer: systematic process of recording, classifying, summarising and communicating financial information for decision-making
rubric: Accounting encompasses recording, classifying, summarising and reporting financial data to help stakeholders make decisions.

subject: Accounting
stem: The accounting equation is
options: Assets = Capital - Liabilities|Assets = Capital + Liabilities|Liabilities = Assets + Capital|Capital = Assets + Liabilities
answer: Assets = Capital + Liabilities
rubric: Fundamental accounting equation: Assets = Capital + Liabilities. Every transaction maintains this equality.

subject: Accounting
stem: In double-entry bookkeeping, every transaction affects at least
options: one account|two accounts (one debit, one credit of equal amount)|three accounts|four accounts
answer: two accounts (one debit, one credit of equal amount)
rubric: Double entry: each transaction has a debit entry and an equal credit entry, maintaining the accounting equation.

subject: Accounting
stem: Debit means an entry on the
options: right side of an account|left side of an account|top of the balance sheet|bottom of the income statement
answer: left side of an account
rubric: Debit (Dr) is recorded on the LEFT side of a T-account; Credit (Cr) on the RIGHT.

subject: Accounting
stem: Which of the following is an asset?
options: Owner's capital|Bank overdraft|Trade payables|Motor vehicle
answer: Motor vehicle
rubric: Assets are resources owned by the business with future economic benefit. Motor vehicle is a tangible non-current asset.

subject: Accounting
stem: A liability is best described as
options: cash held by the business|an amount owed BY the business to external parties|profit earned|goods in store
answer: an amount owed BY the business to external parties
rubric: Liabilities are obligations — amounts the business owes to creditors, banks, suppliers or lenders.

subject: Accounting
stem: Capital in accounting represents
options: the cash in the business|the owner's equity (net worth) — assets minus liabilities|the total assets|the total liabilities
answer: the owner's equity (net worth) — assets minus liabilities
rubric: Capital = Assets - Liabilities. It represents the owner's investment and retained earnings in the business.

subject: Accounting
stem: Which accounting concept requires that revenue is recognised when earned, not when cash is received?
options: Going concern|Accruals (matching) concept|Prudence|Consistency
answer: Accruals (matching) concept
rubric: The accruals concept: revenues and expenses are recorded in the period they arise, regardless of when cash flows.

subject: Accounting
stem: The going concern concept assumes that
options: the business will cease trading soon|the business will continue in operation for the foreseeable future|assets are valued at market price|all debts will be written off
answer: the business will continue in operation for the foreseeable future
rubric: Going concern: accounts are prepared on the assumption the business will continue trading, justifying non-liquidation values.

subject: Accounting
stem: The prudence (conservatism) concept in accounting states that
options: revenue should be overstated|profits should be anticipated but losses should be provided for when probable|all expenses are optional|assets are always understated
answer: profits should be anticipated but losses should be provided for when probable
rubric: Prudence: do not overstate assets/income; recognise losses/liabilities as soon as they are probable.

subject: Accounting
stem: The consistency concept requires that
options: different methods can be used each year|the same accounting methods are applied from one period to the next|all firms use the same method|no methods can ever be changed
answer: the same accounting methods are applied from one period to the next
rubric: Consistency ensures comparability across periods; if a method changes, it must be disclosed.

subject: Accounting
stem: The materiality concept means that
options: all transactions must be recorded in detail|only transactions significant enough to affect decisions need be separately disclosed|small items are ignored entirely|only large assets appear in accounts
answer: only transactions significant enough to affect decisions need be separately disclosed
rubric: Materiality: minor items may be aggregated or simplified; only information that could influence a user's decision is disclosed separately.

subject: Accounting
stem: Which of the following is a current asset?
options: Motor vehicle|Land and buildings|Trade receivables (debtors)|Long-term investment
answer: Trade receivables (debtors)
rubric: Current assets are expected to be converted to cash within one year: stock, debtors, prepayments, bank, cash.

subject: Accounting
stem: A creditor is a person
options: who owes the business money|to whom the business owes money|who manages accounts|who audits the business
answer: to whom the business owes money
rubric: Creditors (trade payables) are suppliers who have provided goods/services for which the business has not yet paid.

subject: Accounting
stem: A debtor is a person
options: to whom the business owes money|who owes money to the business|who provides goods on credit|who manages the bank account
answer: who owes money to the business
rubric: Debtors (trade receivables) are customers who have received goods/services but not yet paid.

subject: Accounting
stem: The business entity concept requires that
options: the owner's personal transactions are included in the business accounts|the business is treated as separate from its owners for accounting purposes|all businesses use the same accounts|taxes are included in accounts
answer: the business is treated as separate from its owners for accounting purposes
rubric: Business entity: the business has its own separate identity; personal transactions of the owner are excluded.

subject: Accounting
stem: Gross profit is calculated as
options: Revenue - All expenses|Revenue - Cost of goods sold|Net profit + expenses|Capital + liabilities
answer: Revenue - Cost of goods sold
rubric: Gross Profit = Revenue (Sales) - Cost of Goods Sold (COGS). It measures profit before overhead expenses.

subject: Accounting
stem: Net profit is calculated as
options: Gross profit - Other income|Gross profit + expenses|Gross profit - Operating expenses|Revenue - Tax only
answer: Gross profit - Operating expenses
rubric: Net Profit = Gross Profit - Operating Expenses (overheads). It is the final profit after all costs.

subject: Accounting
stem: The money measurement concept states that
options: all assets must be measured in physical units|only transactions and events that can be expressed in monetary terms are recorded in the accounts|future transactions are included|all prices are fixed
answer: only transactions and events that can be expressed in monetary terms are recorded in the accounts
rubric: Money measurement: accounting only records what can be expressed in money — human capital, brand reputation are not recorded.

subject: Accounting
stem: In accounting, the term "depreciation" refers to
options: the increase in value of a fixed asset|the allocation of the cost of a non-current (fixed) asset over its useful life|cash paid for an asset|the insurance on an asset
answer: the allocation of the cost of a non-current (fixed) asset over its useful life
rubric: Depreciation spreads the cost of a tangible asset over the periods it is used, matching expense to the benefit received.

subject: Accounting
stem: Books of original entry (books of prime entry) are used to
options: summarise final accounts|record transactions for the first time before they are posted to the ledger|replace the ledger|record only cash transactions
answer: record transactions for the first time before they are posted to the ledger
rubric: Books of original entry (daybooks, journals) capture transactions in chronological order before double entry in the ledger.

subject: Accounting
stem: The sales journal (sales day book) records
options: all cash sales|all credit sales only|all purchases|all returns
answer: all credit sales only
rubric: The sales day book lists all credit sales invoices; cash sales go to the cash book.

subject: Accounting
stem: The purchases journal records
options: all credit purchases only|all cash purchases|all sales|goods returned
answer: all credit purchases only
rubric: The purchases day book records all invoices received for credit purchases; cash purchases go to the cash book.

subject: Accounting
stem: The sales returns journal (returns inward book) records
options: goods sent back by the business to suppliers|goods returned by customers to the business|all sales|all discounts
answer: goods returned by customers to the business
rubric: Returns inward (sales returns): customers returning goods; credit notes issued reduce debtors and sales.

subject: Accounting
stem: The purchases returns journal records
options: goods returned to the business by customers|goods returned by the business to its suppliers|all cash refunds|all discounts received
answer: goods returned by the business to its suppliers
rubric: Returns outward (purchases returns): the business returns goods to suppliers; debit notes issued reduce creditors and purchases.

subject: Accounting
stem: The cash book serves as both a book of original entry AND
options: a ledger account for cash and bank|only a journal|only a ledger|only a control account
answer: a ledger account for cash and bank
rubric: The cash book is unique: it is both a book of prime entry (for recording cash/bank transactions) and part of the ledger.

subject: Accounting
stem: A petty cash book is used to record
options: large capital purchases|small (petty) cash payments using the imprest system|all credit transactions|overseas payments
answer: small (petty) cash payments using the imprest system
rubric: The petty cash book handles minor expenses (stamps, tea, bus fares) under the imprest system — a fixed float is regularly topped up.

subject: Accounting
stem: The imprest system of petty cash means
options: cash is drawn as needed|a fixed float is maintained; the amount spent is reimbursed to restore the float to its original level|petty cash is unlimited|there is no petty cash book
answer: a fixed float is maintained; the amount spent is reimbursed to restore the float to its original level
rubric: Imprest: the petty cashier holds a fixed sum; at intervals, the exact amount spent is reimbursed, restoring the float.

subject: Accounting
stem: The general journal is used to record transactions that
options: are recorded in other day books|do not belong in any other specialist book (e.g. opening entries, corrections, non-cash adjustments, depreciation)|are only cash|are only credit sales
answer: do not belong in any other specialist book (e.g. opening entries, corrections, non-cash adjustments, depreciation)
rubric: The journal proper handles adjustments, errors, depreciation, bad debts, purchase/sale of fixed assets on credit.

subject: Accounting
stem: A journal entry consists of
options: the date only|the account to be debited, account to be credited, date and narration (brief explanation)|only a narration|only the debit entry
answer: the account to be debited, account to be credited, date and narration (brief explanation)
rubric: Journal entries: Dr account / Cr account / Date / Amount / Narration (explanation of the transaction).

subject: Accounting
stem: When goods worth N50,000 are sold on credit to Ade, the correct journal entry is
options: Dr Sales; Cr Ade|Dr Ade; Cr Sales|Dr Cash; Cr Sales|Dr Sales; Cr Cash
answer: Dr Ade; Cr Sales
rubric: Credit sale: Ade (debtor) receives goods → Dr Ade's account (asset increases); Sales revenue earned → Cr Sales account.

subject: Accounting
stem: When goods are purchased on credit from Bello, the correct journal entry is
options: Dr Purchases; Cr Cash|Dr Cash; Cr Bello|Dr Purchases; Cr Bello|Dr Bello; Cr Purchases
answer: Dr Purchases; Cr Bello
rubric: Credit purchase: Purchases (expense) increases → Dr Purchases; Bello (creditor/liability) increases → Cr Bello.

subject: Accounting
stem: A source document for the sales journal is
options: a purchase invoice from a supplier|a sales invoice issued to a customer|a bank statement|a receipt from a customer
answer: a sales invoice issued to a customer
rubric: Each credit sale is recorded from the sales invoice; the invoice is the source document for the sales day book.

subject: Accounting
stem: Totals from the sales journal are posted to the ledger as
options: Dr individual debtors; Cr Sales (total)|Dr Sales; Cr individual debtors|Dr Cash; Cr Sales|Dr Sales; Cr Cash
answer: Dr individual debtors; Cr Sales (total)
rubric: Each invoice: Dr individual debtor's account. Periodically, total sales: Cr Sales account in the general ledger.

subject: Accounting
stem: The folio column in a book of original entry is used to
options: record dates|cross-reference the page number of the corresponding ledger account|record the amount|record the name
answer: cross-reference the page number of the corresponding ledger account
rubric: Folio references link each entry in the daybook to its corresponding ledger account page, aiding audit trail.

subject: Accounting
stem: Contra entries in the cash book occur when
options: cash is sold|money is moved between the cash account and the bank account within the business|two customers pay|a cheque is dishonoured
answer: money is moved between the cash account and the bank account within the business
rubric: Contra entries appear on both sides of the cash book: e.g. cash banked → Cr Cash column, Dr Bank column (same book).

subject: Accounting
stem: A dishonoured cheque is a cheque that
options: has been cashed|the bank refuses to honour (pay) because of insufficient funds or other reasons|is crossed|is post-dated and valid
answer: the bank refuses to honour (pay) because of insufficient funds or other reasons
rubric: A dishonoured (bounced) cheque reverses the original receipt entry: Dr Debtor (or Dr relevant account); Cr Bank.

subject: Accounting
stem: When a debtor is allowed a discount for early payment, this is recorded as
options: Dr Discount Allowed; Cr Debtors|Dr Debtors; Cr Discount Allowed|Dr Cash; Cr Discount|Dr Discount; Cr Cash
answer: Dr Discount Allowed; Cr Debtors
rubric: Discount allowed reduces debtors and is an expense: Dr Discount Allowed (expense), Cr Debtors (reduces asset).

subject: Accounting
stem: Discount received from a supplier is recorded as
options: Dr Purchases; Cr Discount Received|Dr Discount Received; Cr Creditors|Dr Creditors; Cr Discount Received|Dr Cash; Cr Discount
answer: Dr Creditors; Cr Discount Received
rubric: Discount received reduces the creditor balance and is income: Dr Creditors (reduces liability), Cr Discount Received (income).

subject: Accounting
stem: The purchases returns journal total is posted as
options: Dr Purchases Returns; Cr Creditors (total)|Dr Creditors (total); Cr Purchases Returns|Dr Cash; Cr Returns|Dr Returns; Cr Sales
answer: Dr Creditors (total); Cr Purchases Returns
rubric: Returns outward: Dr individual creditor (reduces creditor); periodically total: Cr Purchases Returns account.

subject: Accounting
stem: Which of the following would NOT appear in the cash book?
options: Cash received from a customer|Cheque issued to a supplier|A credit sale to a customer|Bank charges debited by the bank
answer: A credit sale to a customer
rubric: Cash book records cash and bank movements; a credit sale involves no immediate cash — it goes in the sales day book.

subject: Accounting
stem: Opening entries for a new business are recorded in
options: the sales journal|the general journal|the cash book only|the purchases journal
answer: the general journal
rubric: When a business opens, initial assets and liabilities are recorded via journal entries — the general journal handles such non-routine entries.

subject: Accounting
stem: The three-column cash book has columns for
options: only cash|cash, bank and discount|cash only on the debit side|purchases, sales and returns
answer: cash, bank and discount
rubric: The three-column cash book has: Discount | Cash | Bank on both the debit (receipts) and credit (payments) sides.

subject: Accounting
stem: Carriage inwards is the cost of
options: delivering goods to customers|transporting purchased goods to the business|insuring goods in transit|exporting goods
answer: transporting purchased goods to the business
rubric: Carriage inwards: freight cost of bringing purchases into the business; it is added to cost of purchases.

subject: Accounting
stem: Carriage outwards is the cost of
options: bringing goods into the business|delivering sold goods to customers|insuring exports|raw material transport only
answer: delivering sold goods to customers
rubric: Carriage outwards: cost of delivering goods to customers; it is an expense in the income statement (not added to COGS).

subject: Accounting
stem: The ledger is best described as
options: a book of original entry|the principal book of account containing all accounts classified as assets, liabilities, capital, income and expenses|a bank statement|a list of debtors
answer: the principal book of account containing all accounts classified as assets, liabilities, capital, income and expenses
rubric: The ledger is the main book: every account has its own T-account page; posting from daybooks updates each account.

subject: Accounting
stem: A T-account is divided into two sides: the left (debit) side and the right (credit) side. An asset account increases on the
options: credit side|debit side|both sides equally|neither side
answer: debit side
rubric: DEAD CLIC rule: Debit increases: Expenses, Assets, Drawings. Credit increases: Liabilities, Income, Capital.

subject: Accounting
stem: A liability account increases on the
options: debit side|credit side|both sides|left side
answer: credit side
rubric: Liabilities increase with a Credit entry; they decrease with a Debit entry.

subject: Accounting
stem: An income (revenue) account increases on the
options: debit side|credit side|both sides|neither side
answer: credit side
rubric: Revenue accounts increase on the credit side; they are closed to profit and loss at period end.

subject: Accounting
stem: An expense account increases on the
options: credit side|debit side|both sides|neither side
answer: debit side
rubric: Expense accounts increase with debits (cost incurred); they are closed to profit and loss at period end.

subject: Accounting
stem: Balancing a ledger account means
options: deleting all entries|finding the difference between total debits and total credits to find the closing balance|adding all entries|paying off all debts
answer: finding the difference between total debits and total credits to find the closing balance
rubric: Balancing: total each side, write in the difference as the balance c/d (carried down), then bring it forward (b/d) next period.

subject: Accounting
stem: "Balance b/d" in a ledger account means
options: balance brought forward from the previous period (opening balance)|balance carried forward to next period|bank balance only|balance of discounts
answer: balance brought forward from the previous period (opening balance)
rubric: b/d = brought down (opening balance from last period). c/d = carried down (closing balance at period end).

subject: Accounting
stem: The sales ledger (debtors ledger) contains
options: accounts of suppliers|accounts of customers (debtors) who owe the business money|only cash accounts|only bank accounts
answer: accounts of customers (debtors) who owe the business money
rubric: The sales ledger holds individual debtor accounts — each customer's account shows amounts owed.

subject: Accounting
stem: The purchases ledger (creditors ledger) contains
options: accounts of customers|accounts of suppliers (creditors) to whom the business owes money|only asset accounts|only expense accounts
answer: accounts of suppliers (creditors) to whom the business owes money
rubric: The purchases ledger holds individual creditor accounts — each supplier's account shows amounts owed to them.

subject: Accounting
stem: The general (nominal) ledger contains
options: only debtor accounts|only creditor accounts|all accounts except individual debtor/creditor accounts (assets, liabilities, capital, income, expenses)|only bank accounts
answer: all accounts except individual debtor/creditor accounts (assets, liabilities, capital, income, expenses)
rubric: The general ledger holds impersonal accounts: assets, liabilities, capital, revenues, expenses — the backbone of the accounts.

subject: Accounting
stem: When a debtor pays cash, the double entry is
options: Dr Cash; Cr Sales|Dr Cash; Cr Debtor's account|Dr Debtor; Cr Cash|Dr Sales; Cr Cash
answer: Dr Cash; Cr Debtor's account
rubric: Receipt from debtor: Cash (asset) increases → Dr Cash; Debtor (asset) decreases → Cr Debtor's account.

subject: Accounting
stem: Bad debts written off are recorded as
options: Dr Bad Debts Expense; Cr Debtors|Dr Debtors; Cr Bad Debts|Dr Cash; Cr Bad Debts|Dr Bad Debts; Cr Cash
answer: Dr Bad Debts Expense; Cr Debtors
rubric: Bad debt write-off: Dr Bad Debts (expense) to record the loss; Cr Debtor's account (removes the uncollectable asset).

subject: Accounting
stem: A provision for doubtful debts is created because
options: all debtors will pay|some debtors may not pay, so a prudent estimate of likely bad debts is recognised in advance|the business has no debtors|it is required by tax law only
answer: some debtors may not pay, so a prudent estimate of likely bad debts is recognised in advance
rubric: Provision for doubtful debts applies the prudence concept: anticipate expected credit losses without waiting for actual default.

subject: Accounting
stem: When a bad debt previously written off is recovered, the entry is
options: Dr Bad Debts; Cr Cash|Dr Cash; Cr Bad Debts Recovered (income) — and re-debit the debtor then credit on receipt|Dr Debts; Cr Capital|Dr Profit; Cr Cash
answer: Dr Cash; Cr Bad Debts Recovered (income) — and re-debit the debtor then credit on receipt
rubric: Recovery: reinstate the debtor (Dr Debtors; Cr Bad Debts Recovered), then record the cash receipt (Dr Cash; Cr Debtors).

subject: Accounting
stem: Drawing account records
options: the owner's salary expense|amounts withdrawn from the business by the owner for personal use|tax payments|purchases of fixed assets
answer: amounts withdrawn from the business by the owner for personal use
rubric: Drawings: owner withdraws cash or goods; Dr Drawings (reduces capital); Cr Cash/Goods account.

subject: Accounting
stem: At year end, the drawings account is closed by transferring it to
options: Profit and Loss account|Capital account (reducing it)|Sales account|Expense account
answer: Capital account (reducing it)
rubric: Drawings are not an expense; they reduce owner's equity: Dr Capital; Cr Drawings to close.

subject: Accounting
stem: Posting refers to the process of
options: recording in the daybook|transferring entries from the books of original entry to the ledger accounts|preparing a trial balance|closing accounts
answer: transferring entries from the books of original entry to the ledger accounts
rubric: Posting: each daybook entry is transferred (posted) to the appropriate debit and credit accounts in the ledger.

subject: Accounting
stem: An account showing a debit balance usually represents
options: a liability or income|an asset or expense|capital only|a creditor
answer: an asset or expense
rubric: Assets and expenses normally have debit balances; liabilities, capital and income normally have credit balances.

subject: Accounting
stem: The capital account of a sole trader increases when
options: the owner makes drawings|the owner introduces additional capital or net profit is transferred|losses are made|liabilities increase
answer: the owner introduces additional capital or net profit is transferred
rubric: Capital increases with: new capital introduced (Cr Capital), and net profit added at year-end (Cr Capital).

subject: Accounting
stem: The nominal ledger account for rent received shows
options: rent paid as a debit|rent received as a credit (income)|only the landlord's personal account|nothing until year end
answer: rent received as a credit (income)
rubric: Rent received is income: Cr Rent Received account; Dr Cash/Bank. At year end, transferred to Profit and Loss.

subject: Accounting
stem: A trial balance is prepared to
options: replace the ledger|check the arithmetic accuracy of the ledger by listing all debit and credit balances and verifying they are equal|calculate profit|show cash flow
answer: check the arithmetic accuracy of the ledger by listing all debit and credit balances and verifying they are equal
rubric: A trial balance lists all ledger account balances; if total debits = total credits, arithmetic posting is likely correct.

subject: Accounting
stem: Which of the following errors is NOT revealed by a trial balance?
options: An entry posted to the wrong side (debit/credit reversal)|A complete omission of a transaction (error of omission)|An entry in the wrong account but correct type (error of commission)|All of the above are not revealed
answer: An error of commission (entry in the wrong account but correct type)
rubric: Errors revealed: arithmetic, posting to wrong side, wrong amount on one side. NOT revealed: omission, commission, compensating, reversal of entries.

subject: Accounting
stem: An error of omission occurs when
options: a transaction is recorded on the wrong side|a transaction is completely left out of the books|the wrong amount is used|the wrong account is used
answer: a transaction is completely left out of the books
rubric: Errors of omission are not shown by the trial balance because both the debit and credit were missed equally.

subject: Accounting
stem: An error of principle occurs when
options: a transaction is omitted|a transaction is recorded in the wrong class of account (e.g. treating a capital item as revenue)|the amount is wrong|posting is reversed
answer: a transaction is recorded in the wrong class of account (e.g. treating a capital item as revenue)
rubric: Error of principle: using wrong account type — e.g. debiting motor vehicle repairs to Motor Vehicles account (capital vs revenue).

subject: Accounting
stem: A compensating error occurs when
options: one error cancels out another error of equal amount, so the trial balance still balances|only one entry is made|both entries are on the same side|the wrong amount is used everywhere
answer: one error cancels out another error of equal amount, so the trial balance still balances
rubric: Two separate errors that happen to cancel each other hide both mistakes from the trial balance.

subject: Accounting
stem: In a trial balance, which accounts appear on the debit side?
options: Liabilities and income|Assets and expenses (plus drawings)|Capital and creditors|All accounts
answer: Assets and expenses (plus drawings)
rubric: Debit balances: assets, expenses, drawings. Credit balances: liabilities, capital, income.

subject: Accounting
stem: A suspense account is opened when
options: the trial balance agrees|the trial balance does not agree — a temporary account holds the difference while errors are located|a new business starts|depreciation is calculated
answer: the trial balance does not agree — a temporary account holds the difference while errors are located
rubric: A suspense account absorbs the imbalance; errors are corrected by journal entries that reduce the suspense balance to zero.

subject: Accounting
stem: Which of the following would cause a trial balance to disagree?
options: Error of omission|Error of commission|Entering a debit entry on the credit side of one account|Compensating error
answer: Entering a debit entry on the credit side of one account
rubric: A single-sided error (posting to wrong side, wrong amount on one side) upsets the debit/credit equality.

subject: Accounting
stem: The trial balance is extracted from
options: the cash book only|all ledger accounts — each account's closing balance is listed|the bank statement|the profit and loss account
answer: all ledger accounts — each account's closing balance is listed
rubric: Every ledger account provides its closing balance for the trial balance; the TB is a list of all these balances.

subject: Accounting
stem: An error of reversal (complete reversal of entry) means that
options: only one entry was made|the correct accounts were used but debit and credit were swapped (Dr where Cr should be, and vice versa)|the amounts are wrong|the account names are wrong
answer: the correct accounts were used but debit and credit were swapped (Dr where Cr should be, and vice versa)
rubric: A complete reversal puts the transaction on the wrong sides of both accounts — not detected by TB as both sides are affected equally.

subject: Accounting
stem: If the trial balance shows total debits of N500,000 and total credits of N496,000, the difference of N4,000 is posted to the
options: Profit account|Suspense account|Capital account|Cash account
answer: Suspense account
rubric: The N4,000 difference is a temporary debit to the suspense account; it must be investigated and errors corrected.

subject: Accounting
stem: Accrued expenses (amounts owing) appear in the trial balance on the
options: debit side|credit side|both sides|neither side
answer: credit side
rubric: Accruals (outstanding expenses) are a current liability → credit balance in the trial balance.

subject: Accounting
stem: Prepaid expenses (payments in advance) appear in the trial balance on the
options: credit side|debit side (current asset)|both sides|neither side
answer: debit side (current asset)
rubric: Prepayments are assets (future benefit paid in advance) → debit balance.

subject: Accounting
stem: Income received in advance (deferred income) appears in the trial balance on the
options: debit side|credit side (current liability)|both sides|neither side
answer: credit side (current liability)
rubric: Income received in advance is a liability (service not yet provided) → credit balance.

subject: Accounting
stem: An extended trial balance (ETB) helps prepare final accounts by adding
options: only the cash column|adjustments columns for accruals, prepayments and depreciation alongside the TB, producing adjusted P&L and balance sheet columns|only the bank column|only the capital column
answer: adjustments columns for accruals, prepayments and depreciation alongside the TB, producing adjusted P&L and balance sheet columns
rubric: The ETB extends the TB with adjustments and then sorts each line into income statement or balance sheet columns.

subject: Accounting
stem: The trading account is used to calculate
options: net profit|gross profit (revenue minus cost of goods sold)|cash flow|capital
answer: gross profit (revenue minus cost of goods sold)
rubric: Trading Account: Sales - COGS = Gross Profit. COGS = Opening Stock + Purchases + Carriage Inwards - Closing Stock.

subject: Accounting
stem: Cost of goods sold (COGS) is calculated as
options: Opening stock + Purchases + Carriage inwards - Closing stock|Sales - Expenses|Total assets - Liabilities|Capital + Drawings
answer: Opening stock + Purchases + Carriage inwards - Closing stock
rubric: COGS formula: Opening Stock + Net Purchases (+ Carriage In) - Closing Stock = Cost of Goods Sold.

subject: Accounting
stem: The profit and loss account shows
options: only gross profit|net profit (gross profit minus all other operating expenses, plus other income)|only revenue|the balance sheet total
answer: net profit (gross profit minus all other operating expenses, plus other income)
rubric: P&L: Gross Profit + Other Income - Expenses = Net Profit. This is the income statement for a trading business.

subject: Accounting
stem: Which of the following appears in the profit and loss account (not the trading account)?
options: Sales revenue|Purchases|Rent expense|Closing stock
answer: Rent expense
rubric: Rent is an overhead (operating expense) appearing in P&L. Sales and purchases appear in the trading account.

subject: Accounting
stem: The balance sheet shows
options: profit for the year only|the financial position of a business at a specific date — assets, liabilities and capital|cash receipts and payments|revenue and expenses
answer: the financial position of a business at a specific date — assets, liabilities and capital
rubric: The balance sheet (statement of financial position) is a snapshot at one date: Assets = Capital + Liabilities.

subject: Accounting
stem: Non-current (fixed) assets on the balance sheet include
options: cash at bank|debtors|land, buildings, machinery and equipment|stock
answer: land, buildings, machinery and equipment
rubric: Non-current assets are held for long-term use in the business: land, buildings, motor vehicles, plant and equipment.

subject: Accounting
stem: Current liabilities on the balance sheet include
options: long-term loans|share capital|trade payables (creditors) and bank overdrafts|motor vehicles
answer: trade payables (creditors) and bank overdrafts
rubric: Current liabilities are due within one year: trade creditors, accruals, bank overdraft, current portion of long-term debt.

subject: Accounting
stem: Net current assets (working capital) is calculated as
options: Total assets - Total liabilities|Current assets - Current liabilities|Fixed assets - Long-term liabilities|Capital - Drawings
answer: Current assets - Current liabilities
rubric: Working capital = Current Assets - Current Liabilities. Positive working capital means the business can meet short-term obligations.

subject: Accounting
stem: Closing stock appears in the final accounts as
options: a debit in the trading account AND a current asset in the balance sheet|only in the P&L|only in the balance sheet|only in the trading account
answer: a debit in the trading account AND a current asset in the balance sheet
rubric: Closing stock: Cr Trading Account (reduces COGS) AND Dr Balance Sheet as current asset.

subject: Accounting
stem: An accrued expense (e.g. unpaid wages at year end) is shown in the final accounts as
options: an additional debit in P&L AND a current liability in the balance sheet|only in P&L|only in the balance sheet|a non-current asset
answer: an additional debit in P&L AND a current liability in the balance sheet
rubric: Accrual: add to the expense in P&L (Dr Wages) AND show as a current liability in the Balance Sheet (Cr Accruals).

subject: Accounting
stem: A prepaid expense (e.g. insurance paid in advance) is shown as
options: an addition to expenses in P&L|only in the balance sheet|a reduction in the expense in P&L AND a current asset in the balance sheet|a current liability
answer: a reduction in the expense in P&L AND a current asset in the balance sheet
rubric: Prepayment: deduct from the expense in P&L AND show as a current asset in the Balance Sheet.

subject: Accounting
stem: Depreciation is charged to
options: the balance sheet only|the profit and loss account as an expense, AND the fixed asset is reduced in the balance sheet|capital account only|the sales account
answer: the profit and loss account as an expense, AND the fixed asset is reduced in the balance sheet
rubric: Depreciation: Dr Depreciation Expense (P&L) and Cr Accumulated Depreciation (reduces asset in balance sheet).

subject: Accounting
stem: Which depreciation method charges an equal (fixed) amount each year?
options: Reducing balance method|Straight-line method|Sum-of-years digits method|Units of production method
answer: Straight-line method
rubric: Straight-line: Annual depreciation = (Cost - Residual Value) / Useful Life. Same amount every year.

subject: Accounting
stem: The reducing balance method of depreciation charges a fixed percentage on the
options: original cost every year|reducing (net book) value each year|cost minus residual value|annual profit
answer: reducing (net book) value each year
rubric: Reducing balance: charge is higher in early years, declining over time — suitable for assets that lose value fastest when new.

subject: Accounting
stem: Net book value (NBV) of a fixed asset is
options: cost plus accumulated depreciation|cost minus accumulated depreciation|the market value|the resale price
answer: cost minus accumulated depreciation
rubric: NBV = Cost - Accumulated Depreciation. It is the carrying amount of the asset in the balance sheet.

subject: Accounting
stem: If a fixed asset is sold for more than its net book value, the difference is
options: a loss on disposal|a profit (gain) on disposal shown as income in P&L|added to the asset account|ignored
answer: a profit (gain) on disposal shown as income in P&L
rubric: Profit on disposal = Sale proceeds - NBV. It is credited to the P&L as other income.

subject: Accounting
stem: Gross profit margin is calculated as
options: (Net Profit / Revenue) x 100|(Gross Profit / Revenue) x 100|(Revenue / Cost) x 100|(Assets / Capital) x 100
answer: (Gross Profit / Revenue) x 100
rubric: Gross Profit Margin (%) = (Gross Profit / Revenue) x 100. Measures how efficiently the business generates gross profit from sales.

subject: Accounting
stem: Net profit margin is calculated as
options: (Gross Profit / Revenue) x 100|(Net Profit / Revenue) x 100|(Expenses / Revenue) x 100|(Capital / Revenue) x 100
answer: (Net Profit / Revenue) x 100
rubric: Net Profit Margin (%) = (Net Profit / Revenue) x 100. Measures overall profitability after all costs.

subject: Accounting
stem: Return on capital employed (ROCE) is
options: (Net Profit / Capital Employed) x 100|(Revenue / Assets) x 100|(Gross Profit / Sales) x 100|(Expenses / Capital) x 100
answer: (Net Profit / Capital Employed) x 100
rubric: ROCE measures how efficiently capital generates profit; higher ROCE = better return on investment.

subject: Accounting
stem: The current ratio is calculated as
options: Current assets / Total assets|Current assets / Current liabilities|Total assets / Total liabilities|Net profit / Capital
answer: Current assets / Current liabilities
rubric: Current ratio = CA / CL. A ratio above 1 suggests the business can cover short-term debts; ideal is typically 1.5–2.

subject: Accounting
stem: The quick (acid test) ratio excludes which current asset from its calculation?
options: Debtors|Cash|Stock (inventory)|Prepayments
answer: Stock (inventory)
rubric: Quick ratio = (Current Assets - Stock) / Current Liabilities. Excludes stock as it may not be quickly converted to cash.

subject: Accounting
stem: Revenue expenditure is expenditure that
options: is capitalised as an asset|is incurred in the day-to-day running of the business and is charged to the P&L in the current period|adds to the value of a fixed asset|is paid only once
answer: is incurred in the day-to-day running of the business and is charged to the P&L in the current period
rubric: Revenue expenditure: routine operating costs (wages, rent, repairs) that benefit the current period only — charged to P&L.

subject: Accounting
stem: Capital expenditure is expenditure that
options: appears in the P&L as an expense|is incurred on acquiring or improving fixed assets and is capitalised in the balance sheet|is repeated monthly|is paid to employees
answer: is incurred on acquiring or improving fixed assets and is capitalised in the balance sheet
rubric: Capital expenditure: buying or improving fixed assets (machinery, buildings) — shown as assets in the balance sheet.

subject: Accounting
stem: The statement of affairs is prepared when
options: a full set of ledger accounts is available|single-entry (incomplete) records are used; it estimates capital from assets minus liabilities|the business is profitable|a tax return is filed
answer: single-entry (incomplete) records are used; it estimates capital from assets minus liabilities
rubric: Statement of affairs: used in incomplete records to find opening/closing capital: Capital = Assets - Liabilities.

subject: Accounting
stem: In the balance sheet, share capital and reserves together constitute
options: total assets|non-current assets|shareholders equity (owners equity)|total liabilities
answer: shareholders equity (owners equity)
rubric: Share capital + Retained profits + Other reserves = Shareholders' equity, representing owners' stake in the company.

subject: Accounting
stem: Retained profit (retained earnings) represents
options: dividends paid to shareholders|profit after tax that is kept in the business and not distributed as dividends|the cost of goods sold|the opening stock
answer: profit after tax that is kept in the business and not distributed as dividends
rubric: Retained earnings accumulate year on year; they increase equity and finance future growth without new borrowing.

subject: Accounting
stem: A dividend is a payment made to
options: creditors|shareholders out of the company's profits|the tax authority|employees
answer: shareholders out of the company's profits
rubric: Dividends are distributions of profit to shareholders; declared by the board and paid per share held.

subject: Accounting
stem: The appropriation account for a sole trader shows how net profit is
options: calculated from sales|distributed between drawings and retained capital|paid to creditors|calculated from gross profit
answer: distributed between drawings and retained capital
rubric: Appropriation: Net Profit - Drawings = Net addition to Capital. It bridges P&L and Balance Sheet capital section.

subject: Accounting
stem: Stock turnover ratio measures
options: profit per unit sold|(Cost of Goods Sold / Average Stock) — how many times stock is sold and replaced in a period|cash at bank|return on capital
answer: (Cost of Goods Sold / Average Stock) — how many times stock is sold and replaced in a period
rubric: Stock turnover = COGS / Average Stock. High turnover suggests fast-moving stock; low turnover may indicate slow sales or obsolescence.

subject: Accounting
stem: Debtor collection period (debtor days) measures
options: how fast suppliers are paid|(Debtors / Credit Sales) x 365 — the average number of days debtors take to pay|gross profit rate|stock turnover
answer: (Debtors / Credit Sales) x 365 — the average number of days debtors take to pay
rubric: Debtor days = (Debtors / Credit Sales) x 365. Fewer days = faster collection = better cash flow.

subject: Accounting
stem: A bank reconciliation statement is prepared to
options: balance the cash book|explain the difference between the cash book (bank column) balance and the bank statement balance|calculate profit|prepare final accounts
answer: explain the difference between the cash book (bank column) balance and the bank statement balance
rubric: Bank reconciliation: the two records (cash book and bank statement) often differ due to timing differences and bank charges.

subject: Accounting
stem: Unpresented (outstanding) cheques are cheques that
options: have been returned unpaid|have been issued by the business but not yet cleared through the bank|have been cancelled|are post-dated beyond the year
answer: have been issued by the business but not yet cleared through the bank
rubric: Unpresented cheques are debited in the cash book but not yet on the bank statement; they reduce the bank statement balance.

subject: Accounting
stem: Deposits in transit (lodgements not yet credited) are
options: deposits recorded in the bank statement but not in the cash book|deposits entered in the cash book but not yet appearing on the bank statement|dishonoured cheques|bank charges
answer: deposits entered in the cash book but not yet appearing on the bank statement
rubric: Deposits in transit are receipts recorded by the business but the bank has not yet processed them.

subject: Accounting
stem: Bank charges appear on the bank statement but not in the cash book because
options: the bank makes mistakes|the business was not notified in advance; they must be entered in the cash book as a credit (reducing bank balance)|they are not real|they are tax deductible
answer: the business was not notified in advance; they must be entered in the cash book as a credit (reducing bank balance)
rubric: Bank charges are debited by the bank on the statement; the business must update its cash book accordingly.

subject: Accounting
stem: Interest credited by the bank on a savings-linked account appears on the bank statement but not in the cash book; it should be
options: ignored|entered as a debit in the cash book (increasing bank balance)|removed from the bank statement|shown as a liability
answer: entered as a debit in the cash book (increasing bank balance)
rubric: Interest received: the bank credits the account; the business must Dr Cash Book (bank column); Cr Interest Received.

subject: Accounting
stem: A direct debit (standing order) paid by the bank appears on the bank statement but may not be in the cash book because
options: the business made an error|the business may not have recorded it yet; it must be entered in the cash book as a credit|the bank made an error|it is not a real payment
answer: the business may not have recorded it yet; it must be entered in the cash book as a credit
rubric: Standing orders/direct debits are automatic payments; if not in the cash book, they must be entered as cash book credits.

subject: Accounting
stem: Starting from an updated cash book balance, the bank reconciliation reconciles to the bank statement balance by
options: adding unpresented cheques and deducting deposits in transit|adding deposits in transit and deducting unpresented cheques|adding all bank charges|deducting all deposits
answer: adding deposits in transit and deducting unpresented cheques
rubric: Bank Rec from cash book to bank statement: + deposits in transit (bank doesn't have yet) - unpresented cheques (bank will pay).

subject: Accounting
stem: A credit balance on the bank statement means
options: the business owes the bank money (overdraft)|the bank owes the business money (favourable balance)|the business has made a loss|total debits exceed credits
answer: the bank owes the business money (favourable balance)
rubric: Credit balance on statement = bank owes business; debit balance on statement = overdraft (business owes bank).

subject: Accounting
stem: A debit balance in the bank column of the cash book represents
options: an overdraft|a favourable (positive) bank balance|a loss|a creditor
answer: a favourable (positive) bank balance
rubric: Cash book debit balance (bank column) = positive bank balance. Cash book credit balance = overdraft.

subject: Accounting
stem: An error in the cash book (e.g. a payment entered as N500 instead of N5,000) is corrected by
options: adjusting the bank statement|correcting the cash book entry first, then preparing the bank reconciliation|ignoring it|writing off the difference
answer: correcting the cash book entry first, then preparing the bank reconciliation
rubric: Cash book errors require journal corrections; then the reconciliation uses the corrected cash book balance.

subject: Accounting
stem: A dishonoured cheque reduces
options: the bank statement balance only|the cash book (bank column) balance — Dr Debtors; Cr Bank|the creditors balance|the stock balance
answer: the cash book (bank column) balance — Dr Debtors; Cr Bank
rubric: A bounced cheque reverses the original receipt: the bank debits the account, so cash book must be credited; debtor re-instated.

subject: Accounting
stem: The purpose of updating the cash book before preparing the bank reconciliation is to
options: increase the bank balance|incorporate all bank-initiated items (charges, interest, standing orders) so the cash book is accurate before comparison|remove all timing differences|balance the trial balance
answer: incorporate all bank-initiated items (charges, interest, standing orders) so the cash book is accurate before comparison
rubric: Updating the cash book first ensures all known differences are eliminated; only timing differences remain in the reconciliation.

subject: Accounting
stem: If the bank statement balance is N200,000 and there are unpresented cheques of N30,000 and deposits in transit of N15,000, the adjusted bank balance is
rubric: Bank statement to cash book: deduct unpresented cheques (will leave bank soon) + add deposits in transit = N185,000.

subject: Accounting
stem: Bank errors are errors made by the bank on the bank statement; they are corrected by
options: changing the cash book|notifying the bank; they do NOT affect the cash book|writing them off|adding to creditors
answer: notifying the bank; they do NOT affect the cash book
rubric: Bank errors appear only in the reconciliation statement; the bank is notified to correct the statement; the cash book is correct.

subject: Accounting
stem: In a bank reconciliation, timing differences arise because
options: the business makes errors|different entities record the same transaction at different times|the bank makes errors|the business uses a different currency
answer: different entities record the same transaction at different times
rubric: Timing differences: business records a payment when cheque is written; bank records it when cleared — normal and expected.

subject: Accounting
stem: A favourable cash book balance means
options: the business is overdrawn|the business has money in the bank (asset)|the business has made a profit|stock is high
answer: the business has money in the bank (asset)
rubric: Favourable (positive) balance: business has funds available in the bank account.

subject: Accounting
stem: The adjusted/corrected cash book balance should equal
options: the original cash book balance|the bank statement closing balance (after timing adjustments)|the gross profit|the capital balance
answer: the bank statement closing balance (after timing adjustments)
rubric: After adding back deposits in transit and deducting unpresented cheques from the bank statement, it should match the corrected cash book.

subject: Accounting
stem: Bank reconciliation helps to detect
options: only posting errors|possible fraud, bank errors and missing entries in the cash book|only timing differences|tax evasion
answer: possible fraud, bank errors and missing entries in the cash book
rubric: Reconciliation is a key internal control: it can reveal unauthorised payments, embezzlement or processing errors.

subject: Accounting
stem: Which of the following is NOT a reason for a difference between the cash book and bank statement?
options: Unpresented cheques|Deposits in transit|Bank charges|Gross profit calculation
answer: Gross profit calculation
rubric: Gross profit is a P&L figure; it does not cause a difference between the cash book and bank statement.

subject: Accounting
stem: Standing order payments are set up by the
options: bank on its own|account holder to instruct the bank to pay fixed amounts at regular intervals to a named payee|payee to collect funds|government to collect taxes
answer: account holder to instruct the bank to pay fixed amounts at regular intervals to a named payee
rubric: Standing orders: the account holder pre-authorises recurring fixed payments (e.g. rent, loan instalments).

subject: Accounting
stem: A control account is a summary account in the general ledger that
options: replaces the individual debtor/creditor accounts|records the total of all transactions posted to a subsidiary ledger, confirming the accuracy of that ledger's total|records cash only|records only one transaction
answer: records the total of all transactions posted to a subsidiary ledger, confirming the accuracy of that ledger's total
rubric: Control accounts (total accounts) mirror the total of all individual accounts in the sales or purchases ledger.

subject: Accounting
stem: The sales ledger control account (debtors control) opening balance represents
options: total creditors at the start|the total amount owed by all debtors at the start of the period|opening stock|opening capital
answer: the total amount owed by all debtors at the start of the period
rubric: The opening debit balance = total debtors at the start; it mirrors the total of all individual debtor opening balances.

subject: Accounting
stem: Which of the following is ADDED to the debit side of the sales ledger control account?
options: Cash received from debtors|Returns inwards|Sales (credit sales for the period)|Discounts allowed
answer: Sales (credit sales for the period)
rubric: Dr side of debtors control: opening balance + credit sales + dishonoured cheques. Cr side: receipts, discounts, returns, bad debts.

subject: Accounting
stem: Which of the following is DEDUCTED (credited) in the sales ledger control account?
options: Credit sales|Dishonoured cheques|Returns inwards (goods returned by debtors)|Interest on overdue accounts
answer: Returns inwards (goods returned by debtors)
rubric: Returns inwards reduce debtors: Cr Sales Ledger Control; Dr Sales Returns.

subject: Accounting
stem: The purchases ledger control account (creditors control) opening balance represents
options: total debtors|the total amount owed TO all creditors (suppliers) at the start of the period|opening cash|opening stock
answer: the total amount owed TO all creditors (suppliers) at the start of the period
rubric: Opening credit balance in purchases ledger control = total creditors; the business owes this amount to suppliers.

subject: Accounting
stem: Which of the following is ADDED to the credit side of the purchases ledger control account?
options: Payments to creditors|Purchases returns (returns outward)|Credit purchases for the period|Discounts received
answer: Credit purchases for the period
rubric: Cr side of creditors control: opening balance + credit purchases + interest charged by suppliers. Dr side: payments, discounts, returns.

subject: Accounting
stem: Discounts received are shown in the purchases ledger control account on the
options: credit side (increase creditors)|debit side (reduce the amount owed to creditors)|both sides|neither side
answer: debit side (reduce the amount owed to creditors)
rubric: Discount received reduces the creditor balance: Dr Purchases Ledger Control; Cr Discount Received.

subject: Accounting
stem: The closing balance of the sales ledger control account should equal
options: total creditors|the total of all individual debtor balances in the sales ledger|total assets|total sales
answer: the total of all individual debtor balances in the sales ledger
rubric: If the control account balance = sum of all individual debtor accounts, the sales ledger is arithmetically accurate.

subject: Accounting
stem: A contra entry in the control accounts occurs when
options: a customer is also a supplier; the balance is set off between the two ledgers|two accounts have the same balance|a new customer pays|a discount is allowed
answer: a customer is also a supplier; the balance is set off between the two ledgers
rubric: Contra/set-off: where a person is both a debtor and a creditor, the smaller balance cancels part of the larger.

subject: Accounting
stem: Bad debts written off appear on which side of the sales ledger control account?
options: Debit side|Credit side|Both sides|Neither side
answer: Credit side
rubric: Bad debts reduce debtors: Cr Sales Ledger Control; Dr Bad Debts Expense.

subject: Accounting
stem: The control account concept provides which main benefit?
options: Faster cash collection|Enables errors in the subsidiary ledger to be detected and located more easily|Reduces bank charges|Increases sales
answer: Enables errors in the subsidiary ledger to be detected and located more easily
rubric: Control accounts are an internal check: if the control account total differs from the subsidiary ledger total, an error exists.

subject: Accounting
stem: Interest charged on overdue debtor accounts is added to the
options: credit side of the debtors control|debit side of the debtors control (increases amount owed)|P&L only|balance sheet only
answer: debit side of the debtors control (increases amount owed)
rubric: Interest increases the debtor's balance: Dr Sales Ledger Control; Cr Interest Receivable.

subject: Accounting
stem: Refunds to debtors (cash paid back to debtors) are shown on the
options: debit side of sales ledger control|credit side of sales ledger control|debit side of purchases ledger control|neither control account
answer: credit side of sales ledger control
rubric: A refund reduces net debtors: Dr Debtors account; Cr Cash — so Cr Sales Ledger Control.

subject: Accounting
stem: The purchases ledger control account closing balance represents
options: the total amount owed BY the business to its suppliers|total sales|total assets|net profit
answer: the total amount owed BY the business to its suppliers
rubric: Closing credit balance = total creditors (trade payables) — the business still owes this to suppliers.

subject: Accounting
stem: If the total of the individual debtor balances is N450,000 but the sales ledger control account shows N460,000, the N10,000 difference indicates
options: profit has increased|an error exists in either the control account or individual ledger accounts|a normal timing difference|tax is due
answer: an error exists in either the control account or individual ledger accounts
rubric: The mismatch signals a posting error; the ledger must be checked transaction by transaction to locate the discrepancy.

subject: Accounting
stem: Depreciation is the process of
options: increasing the value of an asset over time|systematically allocating the cost of a non-current asset over its useful economic life|revaluing an asset to market price|insuring an asset against loss
answer: systematically allocating the cost of a non-current asset over its useful economic life
rubric: Depreciation matches the cost of using a fixed asset to the periods it generates revenue (matching concept).

subject: Accounting
stem: Which of the following is NOT a cause of depreciation?
options: Wear and tear from use|Obsolescence (new technology making asset outdated)|Passage of time (e.g. leases)|Increase in demand for the product
answer: Increase in demand for the product
rubric: Depreciation causes: physical wear and tear, obsolescence, time passing (finite life). Demand affects revenue, not asset life.

subject: Accounting
stem: Under the straight-line method, annual depreciation is calculated as
options: Cost x Rate %|(Cost - Residual Value) / Useful Life (years)|Net Book Value x Rate %|Cost / 2
answer: (Cost - Residual Value) / Useful Life (years)
rubric: Straight-line formula: (Cost - Scrap/Residual Value) / Useful life = equal annual charge.

subject: Accounting
stem: A machine costs N1,200,000, has a residual value of N200,000 and a useful life of 5 years. Annual straight-line depreciation is

subject: Accounting
stem: Under the reducing balance method, depreciation is charged at a fixed percentage on the
options: original cost|net book value (reducing each year)|residual value|annual revenue
answer: net book value (reducing each year)
rubric: Reducing balance: Depreciation = NBV x Rate%. As NBV falls each year, the charge also falls — higher in early years.

subject: Accounting
stem: An asset with cost N500,000 is depreciated at 20% reducing balance. Depreciation in Year 1 is
rubric: Year 1: N500,000 x 20% = N100,000. NBV at end of Year 1 = N400,000.

subject: Accounting
stem: Using the same asset (N500,000 at 20% reducing balance), depreciation in Year 2 is
rubric: Year 2: NBV N400,000 x 20% = N80,000. NBV at end of Year 2 = N320,000.

subject: Accounting
stem: The reducing balance method is most appropriate for assets that
options: lose value evenly|lose value faster in early years (e.g. motor vehicles, computers)|have indefinite life|are not physical assets
answer: lose value faster in early years (e.g. motor vehicles, computers)
rubric: Reducing balance front-loads depreciation, matching higher repair costs in later years with lower depreciation — suitable for motor vehicles.

subject: Accounting
stem: Accumulated depreciation is
options: the depreciation charge for the current year only|the total depreciation charged on an asset from purchase to date|the asset's market value|the residual value
answer: the total depreciation charged on an asset from purchase to date
rubric: Accumulated depreciation builds up: each year's charge is added; deducted from cost to get NBV.

subject: Accounting
stem: The journal entry for recording annual depreciation is
options: Dr Fixed Asset; Cr Depreciation Expense|Dr Depreciation Expense; Cr Accumulated Depreciation|Dr Cash; Cr Depreciation|Dr Depreciation; Cr Capital
answer: Dr Depreciation Expense; Cr Accumulated Depreciation
rubric: Depreciation: Dr Depreciation Expense (charge to P&L); Cr Accumulated Depreciation (contra-asset reducing NBV in balance sheet).

subject: Accounting
stem: When a depreciable asset is disposed of, the first step is to
options: credit the accumulated depreciation|debit the disposal account with the cost of the asset and credit the fixed asset account|debit cash only|write off to P&L directly
answer: debit the disposal account with the cost of the asset and credit the fixed asset account
rubric: Step 1 of disposal: Dr Disposal Account (cost); Cr Fixed Asset Account (removes asset at cost).

subject: Accounting
stem: The accumulated depreciation on a disposed asset is transferred to the disposal account by
options: Dr Fixed Asset; Cr Disposal|Dr Disposal; Cr Fixed Asset|Dr Accumulated Depreciation; Cr Disposal Account|Dr Disposal; Cr Cash
answer: Dr Accumulated Depreciation; Cr Disposal Account
rubric: Step 2 of disposal: transfer accumulated depreciation to disposal account: Dr Accumulated Depreciation; Cr Disposal.

subject: Accounting
stem: If proceeds from sale exceed the net book value of an asset, the result is
options: a loss on disposal|a profit on disposal|no effect on P&L|an increase in depreciation
answer: a profit on disposal
rubric: Profit on disposal: proceeds > NBV. Cr Profit on Disposal (income in P&L). If proceeds < NBV: Dr Loss on Disposal.

subject: Accounting
stem: Land is generally NOT depreciated because
options: it is always increasing in value|it has an indefinite useful life and does not wear out|it is too expensive|it is not a fixed asset
answer: it has an indefinite useful life and does not wear out
rubric: Land is not depreciated: it has an unlimited useful life and does not physically wear out (though depletion applies to natural resources).

subject: Accounting
stem: The revaluation method of depreciation is used for assets such as
options: motor vehicles|loose tools, where the closing value is estimated annually and depreciation = opening value + additions - closing value|land|patents
answer: loose tools, where the closing value is estimated annually and depreciation = opening value + additions - closing value
rubric: Revaluation method: used for small tools, crockery, etc. Depreciation = Opening balance + Purchases - Closing inventory value.

subject: Accounting
stem: Amortisation is the term used for depreciation applied to
options: tangible fixed assets like machinery|intangible assets (patents, goodwill, trademarks) and leases|current assets|investments
answer: intangible assets (patents, goodwill, trademarks) and leases
rubric: Amortisation: systematic write-off of intangible assets over their useful life — equivalent to depreciation for tangibles.

subject: Accounting
stem: The provision for depreciation account is a
options: revenue account|liability account|contra-asset account that accumulates total depreciation on an asset|capital account
answer: contra-asset account that accumulates total depreciation on an asset
rubric: Accumulated depreciation is a contra-asset (credit balance): it is deducted from the asset's cost in the balance sheet.

subject: Accounting
stem: The machine costs N900,000, straight-line over 10 years, zero residual value. After 3 years, what is the NBV?
rubric: Annual depreciation = N900,000/10 = N90,000. After 3 years: Accumulated = 3 x N90,000 = N270,000. NBV = N900,000 - N270,000 = N630,000.

subject: Accounting
stem: Which accounting concept most directly supports the charging of depreciation?
options: Business entity|Going concern|Matching (accruals) concept|Materiality
answer: Matching (accruals) concept
rubric: Matching: the cost of using an asset is spread over the periods it generates revenue — depreciation matches cost to benefit.

subject: Accounting
stem: Depreciation does NOT involve
